To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the A2A receptor vasodilator regadenoson produced similar measures of myocardial perfusion as adenosine, but with fewer side effects.
the fixed dose of the vasodilator regadenoson is effective in patients with a range of body sizes.
regadenoson is an effective vasodilator in a wide range of patient body sizes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods to assess myocardial perfusion and metabolism using MRI.
the use of magnetic resonance (MR) imaging to measure the effect of obesity on coronary blood flow.
the effect of body weight on the vasodilatory response to regadenoson in patients undergoing cardiac MRI.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of obesity on myocardial hyperemia during regadenoson administration is not significant and that regadenoson is as good as adenosine in inducing hyperemia.
regadenoson can be used as a stressor in patients with a broad range of BMIs.
regadenoson is as efficacious as adenosine for inducing hyperemia during stress MRI in patients with a broad range of body weights.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
regadenoson is an effective vasodilator in patients of widely varying weight.
regadenoson is an acceptable alternative to adenosine for the assessment of myocardial perfusion with cardiac MRI.
regadenoson is an excellent vasodilator in obese patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that

regadenoson can be used as an alternative to adenosine in patients who cannot receive adenosine due to allergy or side effects, or in patients who cannot be imaged with adenosine due its short duration.
regadenoson is an effective vasodilator in patients with a range of BMI.
the dose of regadenose is not dependent on body weight and that the fixed dose of 0.4 mmol produces maximal hyperemia in subjects with widely varying body mass.
